_comment: Review queue for scripts/scan-candidates.js and the /remote-workers/candidates/ page. Nothing here is a published indicator: a row is a LinkedIn profile that matched one or more heuristic signals associated with DPRK IT-worker persona accounts in public reporting, awaiting a human to open it under an authenticated session and decide. The scanner enforces the one rule that matters -- a URL judged false-positive here is never re-added, and a URL already carried as a confirmed persona in x-dossiers.json / third-party-registries.json / direct-observations.json / scraped-iocs.json is never duplicated into this queue. See the header comment in scripts/scan-candidates.js for the full workflow, and CONTENT_GUIDE.md's citation rule, which this file is deliberately upstream of: nothing in `candidates` may be asserted as a DPRK indicator anywhere else on the site until its status is 'confirmed' and it carries a real source in `corroboration`.

status_values.lead: Matched one or more heuristics below. Not opened under an authenticated session. Not published.
status_values.under-review: Opened under an authenticated session by a human reviewer, who found it worth continued attention but not yet enough to state DPRK affiliation. Not published as an indicator anywhere else on the site.
status_values.confirmed: A human reviewer found independent corroboration -- a cited report, a shared indicator with an existing persona, a password/infrastructure link -- sufficient to state the connection under this site's confidence_level conventions (CONTENT_GUIDE.md). Only a confirmed entry may be promoted into x-dossiers.json or third-party-registries.json as its own persona.
status_values.false-positive: A human reviewer checked the account and found it belongs to an identifiable, uninvolved person, or that the matched heuristics were coincidental. Carries a `reason` and stays in this file permanently so the scanner never re-adds it.

role-title.label: Common DPRK IT-worker role title
role-title.description: Headline or current title is one of a small set of titles that recur across FBI, DOJ, Mandiant, DTEX and KnowBe4 reporting on these operations -- Senior Full Stack Engineer, Senior Software Engineer, Blockchain Developer, and close variants. Weak alone: these are among the most common titles on LinkedIn, held by tens of thousands of real engineers with a real employment history and network.

sparse-history.label: A thin or sparse profile body. Kept for the entries that already cite it, but the two halves of the original wording have separated: account age against claimed experience is the primary signal and has its own entry, while low connection count is weak corroboration at best. See recent-account and seniority-against-empty-network.

ai-photo.label: Likely AI-generated or stock profile photo
ai-photo.description: The profile photograph shows the visual artifacts of AI generation (asymmetric ears/glasses, garbled background text, waxy skin texture, mismatched lighting) or reverse-image-searches to stock photography or an unrelated real person's photo. Requires opening the image at full resolution; cannot be dorked.

vanity-slug-pattern.label: Hand-picked vanity URL slug rather than LinkedIn's default numeric suffix
vanity-slug-pattern.description: LinkedIn assigns a new account a slug of the form firstname-lastname-xxxxxxx (a random alphanumeric suffix) unless the holder deliberately edits it. A slug with no numeric suffix, or one that inserts an unrelated word like 'dev' between two name-shaped segments (e.g. eric-dev-stevens), reflects an edit -- not proof of anything by itself, but a detail worth noting alongside other signals, and one Google indexes and therefore dorkable via inurl:.

open-to-work.label: "Open to Work" banner paired with a senior title and thin content
open-to-work.description: The green Open to Work frame is normal for any job seeker; it only becomes a signal in combination with role-title and sparse-history, which is why it is not scored as an independent heuristic here and is folded into whichever dork query it appears alongside.

reused-employer.label: Employer or company name that recurs across other flagged profiles
reused-employer.description: The claimed current or past employer matches a shell company or a name already seen on another entry in this file or in an existing persona dossier. Requires cross-referencing entries already in this file and in x-dossiers.json / third-party-registries.json; the scanner does not automate this, a reviewer checks it by hand when promoting a lead.

keyword-stuffed-headline.label: A headline that is a run of technology keywords rather than a description of a job, typically ending in a remote-work or availability tag

seniority-against-empty-network.label: A senior title and a long claimed history against a small connection or follower count. TREAT AS CORROBORATION AND NEVER AS A SCREEN: plenty of DPRK IT-worker accounts carry 500+ connections, so a large network rules nothing out and filtering on a small one hides exactly the accounts that have done the work of building a network.

all-roles-remote.label: Every role in the employment history marked remote, including roles dated before remote work was common in that industry

employment-gap.label: An unexplained gap between two consecutive roles in the stated employment history

name-mismatch.label: An account linked from the profile or resume is registered under a name unrelated to the name on the profile

recent-account.label: THE STRONGEST SIGNAL IN THIS FILE. The account was created recently while the profile claims many years of experience — an account eighteen months old asserting a career beginning in 2015, or one made in August claiming continuous employment since 2020. A real engineer with eight years behind them has usually had the account for most of those eight years, because the account is how the career was conducted. Read the join date from LinkedIn's "About this member" panel, which is the only place LinkedIn publishes it: not the profile body, not the contact-info panel.

voip-number.label: The telephone number is an interconnected VoIP line — Skype, Bandwidth, Google Voice and similar — rather than a carrier handset or a fixed line

marketplace-resume.label: The resume was posted as a product listing on a marketplace such as pipu.cc rather than submitted to an employer

llm-reformatted.label: The resume text carries the leaked output of an assistant that reformatted it, which is evidence about whoever uploaded it rather than about the person named on it

indeed-relay.label: The contact address is an @indeedemail.com relay, so the resume was exported from an Indeed application rather than written for this listing

photo-name-mismatch.label: The photograph published with the resume shows a person whose apparent sex does not match the name the resume is filed under. Appearance is not identity and this is an observation rather than a finding, but it means the photograph and the name were not put together by the person in the photograph

group-photograph.label: The image published as the resume's photograph shows several people rather than a single headshot, which is not what an applicant submits and is what a harvested personal photograph looks like

employment-predates-account.label: The employment history claims a role that began before the LinkedIn account itself was created — not impossible for a real person writing up an old job, but it is what a back-filled history looks like

no-profile-photo.label: The account has never set a profile photograph and shows LinkedIn's default silhouette

ocr-letter-substitution.label: The profile text substitutes a lowercase L for a capital I throughout — "Peer Al" for "Peer AI", "Al-driven" for "AI-driven" — which is what text that has been through an image or a copy pipeline looks like, not what somebody typing their own history produces

shared-claimed-employer.label: The account claims an employer also claimed by other accounts of the same shape. The employer is usually a REAL company that the account never worked for, not an invented one, so the signal is the overlap between thin accounts rather than anything about the company

privileged-access-claim.label: The profile claims authority of exactly the kind these operations are known to seek: a multisig signer on a treasury, architect of contracts holding large value, incident response inside a protocol. Not a signal that the account is fake — real engineers hold these roles and write about them — but it raises what is at stake if the account is not what it says, and it belongs in the note for that reason.

real-namesake-account.label: A separate, long-established LinkedIn account exists under the same full name, in the same city, in the same line of work, and the candidate account is the newer of the two. It is the strongest thing short of a cited report, because the alternative explanation -- two engineers of the same name in the same city doing the same job, one of whom made an account this year -- is much harder to hold than the coincidences the other heuristics turn on. It also changes what may be PUBLISHED: the name now belongs to an identifiable uninvolved person, and this file's rule about not naming such a person applies to everything downstream of the row.

duplicate-name-account.label: A second LinkedIn account exists under the same rare name, also recently created, also with an empty network and no profile sections, usually claiming a different employer in a different country. It is not the same finding as real-namesake-account and must not be confused with it: there the older account is an established real person whose identity is being worn, while here neither account is anybody, and what the pair shows is one operator holding more than one identity under a name nobody else has. Established the same way -- a quoted people search on the exact displayed name.

shared-resume-text.label: The resume shares its experience bullets or its skills inventory near-verbatim with a resume filed under a different name, address and telephone number, established by comparing word shingles across every CV in the pipu.cc set rather than by eye. Two applicants do not arrive at the same six-hundred-character list of tools, or the same nine achievement sentences with the percentages shuffled, independently; one hand wrote both. It says who authored the documents, not who the names on them are: where the other resume already belongs to a persona this site holds, the pair is a lead on the operator, and where it does not, the pair is two products of one template.

candidates.name: Eric Stevens
candidates.note: Opened under an authenticated session on 13 September 2026, which corroborated the cache snippet and added considerably to it. The account presents as Eric Stevens, Senior Software Engineer, Los Angeles, under a headline that is a run of twenty keywords ending "Remote | OpenToWork". The About text claims ten years of full-stack and mobile development with an enthusiasm for AI and WEB3. The experience section, which the unauthenticated snippet did not show, names three employers: BARK from April 2022 to the present, Etsy from July 2019 to March 2022, and Insight Global from January 2015 to June 2018, every one of them marked Remote, including the 2015 role. Education is a 2010-2014 BSc in Mathematics and Computer at the National University of Singapore. Against all of that the account holds ONE connection and six followers, has never posted, and is flagged open to work. There is also an unexplained gap between June 2018 and July 2019. The shape matches what this site records elsewhere -- see the Levente Bajusz entry in direct-observations.json, an account LinkedIn dates to May 2025 that back-filled eleven years of employment -- but shape is all it is. No indicator here is shared with any persona the site holds, no cited report names the account, and three real employers are named, which means an error would land on whoever actually holds the name. LinkedIn’s own “About this member” panel, read on 13 September 2026, dates the account to OCTOBER 2024 and shows no verifications, with the contact details and the profile photograph both last changed over a year ago. An account fourteen months old is claiming employment beginning in 2015 and a current role held since April 2022. The profile banner also carries an address the rest of the profile does not, hi.super.eric@gmail.com. Under review, not confirmed. The profile photograph is a real face rather than an illustration or a logo, and is therefore worth an AI-image detector score; none has been run, because the free endpoints now require a key.

fact_fields.account_created: When the account states it was created. For LinkedIn this is the "Joined" date in the "About this member" panel, which is the only place LinkedIn publishes it — the profile body and the contact-info panel do not carry it. For a GitHub account it is the creation date the API gives. Stored as YYYY-MM (or YYYY-MM-DD where the day is known), the ISO form the site uses for dates.
fact_fields.connections: Connection count as the profile displays it.
fact_fields.followers: Follower count as the profile displays it.
fact_fields.claimed_years: Years of experience the profile or resume claims.
fact_fields.employers_named: How many employers the history names.
fact_fields.line_type: Line type of the telephone number on the profile or resume, from a per-number lookup. Three states are distinguished: a value means the lookup resolved; "no-match" means the number was looked up and nothing came back; and no entry at all means no lookup has been run, which the table shows as "Not checked" where a number exists and "N/A" where none does. See docs/phone-line-types.md.
fact_fields.linked_account: An account linked from the profile whose registered name differs from the name on the profile.
fact_fields.source: Where the candidate was surfaced from: a search, or a marketplace listing.
fact_fields.image_check: What the account's OWN avatar turned out to be, and any detector score against it. Nine of ten avatars in this queue are illustrations, logos, screenshots or GitHub's default identicon rather than faces, so there is nothing for a face detector to score on those rows and the AI-generated-photograph heuristic does not apply to them. Where a pipu listing photograph was also examined it is kept here beside the avatar, because the two are different things: the listing photograph is whatever the marketplace was handed, and the avatar is what the account chose to present itself as.
fact_fields.carrier: The carrier behind the telephone number, as the per-number lookup names it.
fact_fields.verifications: Whether LinkedIn shows any identity verification on the account.
fact_fields.links: Every page this candidate can be read on, labelled. A row is rarely one account: a pipu.cc resume has a listing, a GitHub account and often a LinkedIn profile, and a reviewer needs all of them rather than whichever one happened to be picked as the row's main URL.
fact_fields.indicators: Every indicator value the candidate rests on, typed with the same vocabulary the rest of the index uses. Email addresses and telephone numbers come from the pipu.cc listing or from the profile itself; account URLs are repeated here so the row can be read as an indicator set rather than as a link list. A row with no phone_number entry is a row where the source published no number, which is why its line type reads N/A rather than blank.
fact_fields.listing_photo_reuse: Whether the pipu.cc listing's product image is also carried by other listings in the set, from a perceptual hash over every thumbnail (21 September 2026). 519 images each serve two or more listings under different names, so a listing's image is drawn from a pool the uploader used and is not a photograph of the person on the CV; the count is given so the reader can weigh it.
